# How to Translate Menus, Signs and Labels with Your Phone and Gemini

> **In short:** Point your phone camera at any foreign text — a menu, a street sign, a product label — and Gemini will read it and translate it into English in seconds. It usually handles common languages well, though decorative fonts, handwriting, or blurry shots can trip it up.

In a few minutes you'll know how to translate almost any printed text in the world using just your phone and Gemini — Google's AI assistant. This guide is for complete beginners, and assumes you've never opened the app before. All you need is a phone, the app, and a steady hand.

## Before you start

- The **Gemini app** installed (free from the Google Play Store on Android, or the App Store on iPhone).
- A **Google account** signed in on your phone — the same one you'd use for Gmail or YouTube.
- **Camera permission** turned on for the app (your phone will ask the first time).
- A **working internet** connection — Wi-Fi or mobile data. Some translation features need the cloud to work.
- Roughly **2–3 minutes** to translate one thing end-to-end.

A quick honest note: Gemini's camera translation is good for everyday situations, but it won't always be perfect. For anything safety-critical (food allergens, medication labels, legal notices), treat the answer as a starting point and double-check with a human.

## Step 1 — Open Gemini and switch to camera mode

Tap the **Gemini app icon** on your phone — look for a four-pointed spark or star in blue and white. The main chat screen opens with a text box near the bottom. Find the **camera icon** — it usually sits right next to the text box, or tucked inside an attachment menu (a **+** or **paperclip**). Tap it once. A small panel slides up with options like **Take photo** or **Open camera live**. If you only see one option, that's the one to use.

💬 Example: tap the camera icon, then choose **Take photo** if you want a still image, or **Open camera live** if you want to stream what's in front of you.

You'll know it worked when your phone's viewfinder fills the screen, showing what the back camera sees.

## Step 2 — Frame the text and capture it

Hold your phone about **20–30 cm** from the menu, sign, or label — close enough that the text fills about two-thirds of the screen. Try to keep the phone flat and steady, and avoid harsh shadows across the words. If you chose live camera, just point and hold; if you chose photo, tap the round **shutter button** at the bottom of the screen once. Stay still for a moment after the click so the image isn't blurry.

💬 Example: aim so that one menu section, one sign, or one product label fills most of the frame, then tap the round shutter button.

You'll know it worked when Gemini shows the photo (or live video feed) on screen, with a text box ready for your question.

## Step 3 — Ask Gemini to translate

Right below the photo, you'll find a text box — type a short, direct instruction. Mention the source language if you know it, and always say the language you want the answer in (English is the default, but you can ask for others). Press the **send icon** (an arrow or paper plane). Within a few seconds, Gemini replies with the translated text, usually noting what language it spotted.

💬 Example: type **"Translate this menu into English. For each dish, give me the name, a short description, and flag anything containing nuts, dairy, or shellfish."**

You'll know it worked when Gemini's reply contains a clear English version of the text, with any extra details you asked about.

## Step 4 — Ask follow-up questions

If anything is still unclear — a single word, an abbreviation, a cultural reference — just type a follow-up question in the same chat. Gemini remembers the photo and its first answer, so you can dig deeper without re-snapping the picture. Ask things like "what does 'al dente' mean here?", "is this dish usually spicy?", or "which one is the cheapest soup?" You can also ask it to **rewrite the translation over the photo** if you want a visual overlay.

💬 Example: type **"What does the small text under each item say? And which of these soups would you order if you don't like spice?"**

You'll know it worked when Gemini responds with a specific clarification, using the same photo as context — no need to upload anything again.

## Step 5 — Save or share the result

Once the translation looks right, you can keep it, copy it, or send it to someone else. Look for small **icons near Gemini's reply** — usually a **copy** icon (two overlapping squares) and a **share** icon (an arrow pointing up out of a box). Tap **copy** to paste the translation into Notes, Messages, or a translation app. Tap **share** to send it to a friend who's still puzzling over the menu across the table.

💬 Example: tap **copy**, open Notes, then paste — your translated menu is now scrollable on your own screen.

You'll know it worked when the translated text appears in your Notes app (or wherever you pasted it), ready to read at your own pace.

## Common mistakes

- **Tilting the phone so the text is skewed.** Hold the phone flat and face the text straight on. If the photo is already taken at an angle, ask Gemini to "read the text even though it's skewed" — it usually copes.
- **Photographing a dense full page and getting a muddled answer.** A single packed menu is hard for any AI to parse cleanly. Photograph one section at a time, or ask Gemini to "list only the items under 'Pasta'".
- **Trusting the translation without checking the important bits.** Gemini is accurate most of the time, but it can misread a price or miss an allergen. For anything critical (medical, dietary, financial), confirm with a human or an official source.
- **Forgetting to mention the source language.** If the menu mixes two scripts (say, Japanese and English), tell Gemini which part to translate. Otherwise it may try to translate the bits you don't need.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** ordering food abroad, reading street signs while traveling, decoding foreign product labels at the supermarket, or checking the back of a souvenir you just bought.
- **For your business or work:** reading labels on imported goods, understanding signage or documents from overseas clients, or sanity-checking translations before sending them to a customer.
- **If you're just getting started:** don't wait for your next holiday. Try it on the next unfamiliar label or sign you see — the back of a bottle, a product in a specialty shop, anything with foreign text. The first try is the only hard one.

## Try it now

Grab one thing with foreign text near you — a food packet in the cupboard, a souvenir, or even a foreign-language webpage on another screen. Snap it with Gemini, ask for a translation, and read the answer. Two minutes, done.
